newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU states miffed by telecoms report.
newsitem.headline: EU states miffed by telecoms report.

text.p: European Union countries are expected to chastise the European Commission on Friday for the way it graded their efforts to open their telecommunications markets to competition.
Many of them are unhappy with a Commission report that grouped countries according to how well they had complied with the EU's plan to abolish telecoms monopolies by January 1, 1998, diplomats said.
The report, issued in May, gave Britain, Denmark, Finland and Sweden top marks, while saying progress was slowest in Belgium, Greece, Portugal and Spain.

Prompted partly by complaints from the low-ranking countries, EU telecommunications ministers who are meeting in Luxembourg on Friday are set to adopt a statement calling for "an updated and more accurate assessment" of the situation.
Diplomats said states including Portugal, Greece and Italy grumbled about both the content -- saying it did not reflect the actual state of play -- and the tone.
"The Commission should have nothing to do with making a ranking of member states," a Portuguese diplomat said. "(That could) prejudice commercial negotiations."

Since the Commission has granted Portugal the right to delay full liberalisation until the start of 2000 because it has a less developed network, it should not compare the country to those that must follow the earlier timetable, he said.
"Much of what (the report) said was very outdated," a Belgian official said, noting that Belgium adopted a big telecoms liberalisation package just days after the Commission issued its analysis.
"Some of the member states were cross that the Commission didn't say clearly enough that it was a snapshot and only a snapshot," one diplomat said.

The Commission report covered a package of EU directives requiring governments to open their markets in areas ranging from satellite and mobile communications to leased lines and basic voice phone service.
It said it was gearing up to react swiftly to complaints from companies about governments that were not opening up their markets properly.

Jochen Kubosch, a spokesman for EU Telecommunications Commissioner Martin Bangemann, acknowledged that some governments had made progress since the report was issued, which would be reflected in the Commission's next report.
"We're optimistic that because things are moving things will be better for some member states who were criticised," he said.
